hero.title: Heat pumps: do they actually save money over a gas furnace and an air conditioner?
hero.lede: Advocates say a heat pump cuts your bills, works in any winter and pays for itself. Skeptics say it costs a fortune to install, runs up the electric bill when it gets cold, and only pencils out with subsidies that are now gone. This page pulls the testable claims out of videos and articles on both sides and checks each one against national modelling studies, cold-climate field tests, state energy prices, and the tax and rebate rules as they stand in 2026.

recap.bottomLine: a heat pump moves heat instead of burning fuel, so against oil, propane or electric resistance it is reliably cheaper to run. Against natural gas it depends on the ratio of your electricity price to your gas price, on the climate and on how efficient the unit is: national models find most gas homes with central air get lower bills with a good heat pump, but many pay more with a minimum-efficiency one, and a measured UK study found bills rose on a flat tariff and fell on a heat-pump tariff. Upfront, a heat pump costs more than a furnace but about the same as a furnace plus a new air conditioner, so the money case is strongest when the AC also needs replacing and weakest when you tear out a working furnace. Cold-climate field tests show modern units keep heating well below 0°F, though efficiency falls and backup resistance heat can quietly run up bills. The 30% federal tax credit ended for installs after 2025, and since mid-2026 the federal rebate no longer pays to replace gas heating; state and utility rebates remain. {hypeWrong} of {hypeTotal} sweeping promises ("pays for itself in a few years", "cuts bills in half", "most homes save over its life") are judged wrong.
